## Introduction

connector.databricks has two connectors for Databricks tables:

* `ConnectorDatabricksSQL`, created with `connector_databricks_sql()`. It
connects to a SQL warehouse through the `brickster::DatabricksSQL()` DBI driver.
* `ConnectorDatabricksTable`, created with `connector_databricks_table()`. It
connects to a cluster through the `odbc::databricks()` DBI driver.

`ConnectorDatabricksSQL` is the preferred way of working with tables and is
where new development happens. It is marked as experimental, so its interface
may still change. `ConnectorDatabricksTable` is still available for existing
code and for features `ConnectorDatabricksSQL` does not have yet. This article
compares the two and shows how to move from one to the other.

## At a glance

|                         | `ConnectorDatabricksSQL`                                   | `ConnectorDatabricksTable`                                                  |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Constructor             | `connector_databricks_sql(warehouse_id, catalog, schema)`  | `connector_databricks_table(http_path, catalog, schema)`                    |
| DBI driver              | `brickster::DatabricksSQL()`                               | `odbc::databricks()`                                                        |
| Compute                 | The SQL warehouse given by `warehouse_id`                  | The cluster given by `http_path`, and the first SQL warehouse returned by `brickster::db_sql_warehouse_list()` |
| System requirements     | None                                                       | Databricks ODBC driver                                                      |
| Authentication          | brickster                                                  | odbc and brickster                                                          |
| `...` is passed to      | `DBI::dbConnect()` for `brickster::DatabricksSQL()`        | `DBI::dbConnect()` for `odbc::databricks()`                                 |
| `write_cnt()`           | `brickster::dbWriteTable()`, optionally through a staging volume | Always through a temporary volume                                     |
| Appending rows          | `append = TRUE`                                            | Not supported                                                               |
| `read_cnt()`            | `DBI::dbReadTable()`                                       | Arrow results from the SQL warehouse                                        |
| `list_content_cnt()`    | `DBI::dbListTables()`                                      | Unity Catalog API                                                           |
| `remove_cnt()`          | `DBI::dbRemoveTable()`                                     | Unity Catalog API                                                           |
| `tbl_cnt()`             | dbplyr, executed on the SQL warehouse                      | dbplyr, executed on the cluster                                             |
| whirl logging           | Not supported yet                                          | Supported                                                                   |

## Compute and authentication

`ConnectorDatabricksSQL` does everything on one SQL warehouse, and only needs
the brickster authentication described in
[this article](https://databrickslabs.github.io/brickster/articles/setup-auth.html).
No system libraries are needed. `warehouse_id` defaults to the
`DATABRICKS_WAREHOUSE_ID` environment variable, and the IDs of the warehouses
you can use are listed by `brickster::db_sql_warehouse_list()`.

`ConnectorDatabricksTable` opens its DBI connection to the cluster in
`http_path` with `odbc::databricks()`, which needs the Databricks ODBC driver.
That connection is only used by `tbl_cnt()`. Reading, writing, listing,
removing and tagging tables are done with brickster, on the first SQL warehouse
returned by `brickster::db_sql_warehouse_list()`. It therefore needs both odbc
and brickster authentication, and you cannot choose which warehouse is used.
See `vignette("articles/authentication")` for how to set up both.

## Writing

`ConnectorDatabricksSQL` writes with `brickster::dbWriteTable()`. Without a
staging volume the data is sent inside the SQL statement, which is slow for
large data and limited to 50,000 rows. With `staging_volume` set, the data is
uploaded as Parquet files to the volume first. Use a staging volume for
anything but small tables:

```{r staging, eval=FALSE}
con <- connector_databricks_sql(
  warehouse_id = "your-warehouse-id",
  catalog = "my_catalog",
  schema = "my_schema",
  staging_volume = "/Volumes/my_catalog/my_schema/my_volume"
)
```

`ConnectorDatabricksTable` always writes through a temporary volume that it
creates and removes for every write.

See `vignette("articles/read_write")` for details on both.

## Driver parameters

Both constructors pass `...` on to `DBI::dbConnect()` for their driver.

For `ConnectorDatabricksSQL` these are the arguments of the brickster driver,
for example `disposition`, `fetch_timeout`, `max_active_connections`,
`show_progress`, `host` or `token`:

```{r sql_dots, eval=FALSE}
con <- connector_databricks_sql(
  warehouse_id = "your-warehouse-id",
  catalog = "my_catalog",
  schema = "my_schema",
  fetch_timeout = 600,
  show_progress = FALSE
)
```

For `ConnectorDatabricksTable` these are the arguments of `odbc::databricks()`,
for example `workspace`, `uid`, `pwd` or `driver`. `useNativeQuery` defaults to
`FALSE` and can be overridden:

```{r table_dots, eval=FALSE}
con <- connector_databricks_table(
  http_path = "path-to-cluster",
  catalog = "my_catalog",
  schema = "my_schema",
  workspace = "https://my-workspace.cloud.databricks.com"
)
```

## Moving from ConnectorDatabricksTable to ConnectorDatabricksSQL

Replace `http_path` with the ID of the SQL warehouse you want to use. If your
`http_path` already points to a SQL warehouse, it has the form
`/sql/1.0/warehouses/<warehouse-id>` and the last part is the ID.

```{r migrate, eval=FALSE}
# Before
con <- connector_databricks_table(
  http_path = "/sql/1.0/warehouses/abc123",
  catalog = "my_catalog",
  schema = "my_schema"
)

# After
con <- connector_databricks_sql(
  warehouse_id = "abc123",
  catalog = "my_catalog",
  schema = "my_schema"
)
```

In a connector configuration file, change the backend `type` and replace
`http_path` with `warehouse_id`:

```yaml
# Before
datasources:
  - name: "tables"
    backend:
      type: "connector.databricks::connector_databricks_table"
      http_path: "/sql/1.0/warehouses/abc123"
      catalog: "my_catalog"
      schema: "my_schema"

# After
datasources:
  - name: "tables"
    backend:
      type: "connector.databricks::connector_databricks_sql"
      warehouse_id: "abc123"
      catalog: "my_catalog"
      schema: "my_schema"
```

Calls to `read_cnt()`, `write_cnt()`, `list_content_cnt()`, `remove_cnt()` and
`tbl_cnt()` stay the same, except for the `timepoint`, `version` and `tags`
arguments, which `ConnectorDatabricksSQL` does not have. Consider setting
`staging_volume` if you write tables with more than a few thousand rows.
